analysis.one_liner: Bans surprise bills for COVID-19 tests and caps what out-of-network test providers can charge.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced in July 2021 and took no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen existing rules requiring insurers to cover COVID-19 testing with no patient cost-sharing. It would define the "medical management" practices insurers are barred from using to second-guess tests, cap what out-of-network testing providers can be reimbursed at the lower of the cash price or twice the Medicare rate, and make it illegal for providers to bill patients directly for covered tests. It would also require HHS to survey providers' posted cash prices, report on compliance and outlier prices by name, and have three agencies issue guidance so patients aren't hit with cost-sharing or prior-authorization requirements when they get tested.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who got a COVID-19 test — especially those tested at out-of-network sites like freestanding emergency rooms or certain labs — would be protected from surprise bills and from providers trying to collect cost-sharing. Insurers would also gain from a hard cap on out-of-network test reimbursement.

how_it_helps.text: It writes into law that insurers may not use 'medical management' — reviews of why you got tested, whether you had symptoms, who ordered the test, or how often you test — to deny or cost-shift a covered COVID-19 test.

It caps reimbursement for out-of-network testing providers at the lesser of the provider's cash price or twice the Medicare rate, so a lab or freestanding ER cannot charge a plan an unlimited amount that ends up in a patient's bill.
It directly prohibits providers from billing or holding liable any patient for a covered COVID-19 test, closing the gap that produced surprise testing bills during the pandemic.
It raises the civil penalty for violating the testing coverage rules from $300 to $10,000, giving the no-surprise-billing rules real teeth.

It directs HHS to survey at least 200 providers' posted cash prices and publish a report naming providers whose prices are outliers, and requires HHS, Labor, and Treasury to issue guidance clarifying claims so patients face no cost-sharing or prior authorization.

analysis.who_pays: Out-of-network testing providers — hospitals, freestanding emergency rooms, and labs that were charging high prices for COVID tests — would be limited to the cash price or twice the Medicare rate and barred from billing patients. Insurers bear the cost of covering tests without cost-sharing, but the reimbursement cap limits that exposure.

drawbacks.text: The reimbursement cap (lesser of cash price or 2x Medicare) could squeeze smaller labs and rural testing sites if their costs exceeded the cap, potentially narrowing testing access — the same trade-off that made the broader surprise-billing law contentious.

The bill was written while the pandemic was ongoing but most of its protections are tied to the COVID-19 public health emergency framework, so its benefits would fade as the emergency wound down rather than permanently fixing surprise billing for tests generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and targeted: during a pandemic, people were receiving unexpected bills for tests that federal law was supposed to cover for free, and this bill would have closed those loopholes and named the providers charging outlier prices. The main cost falls on providers whose test prices exceeded the cap, and the main honest criticism is that it is a patch tied to the COVID emergency rather than a lasting fix — but as a patch, it is hard to argue against on the merits. Its failure appears procedural, not substantive.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee in July 2021, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the bill on July 21, 2021, with Senator Amy Klobuchar, and it was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
It attracted only one cosponsor over its entire life.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — the referral was the last thing that ever happened to it.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill was never reintroduced history shows it expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Testing providers charging high prices for COVID-19 tests — and the insurers and patients who would have been on the hook for the difference — are all in the position they would have been in anyway, because the rules were never tightened. Patients who received surprise test bills got no relief from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban surprise COVID-19 test bills and cap out-of-network test reimbursement.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only other original sponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to expire when the Congress ended.

against.name: The rest of the Senate
against.what_they_did: No senator beyond the two sponsors signed on, and no senator moved to bring the bill up.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition is on the record; both sponsors were Minnesota Democrats, and the bill simply never moved, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Out-of-network testing providers (labs, freestanding ERs, hospital testing sites)
industries.note: The bill caps what they can be reimbursed for COVID tests at the lesser of their cash price or twice the Medicare rate, and makes it illegal to bill patients directly. Providers whose prices were far above Medicare rates would lose revenue and lose the ability to pursue patients for balances.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: They must continue covering COVID tests with no cost-sharing and no medical management, but the hard reimbursement cap limits their out-of-network costs. Patients are protected from surprise bills either way, so the industry's interest here largely runs alongside the public's.
